reason: The provided sources supply rich, multi-site verified details on Sedna's discovery, extreme 11,000-year orbit, physical properties, and origin theories.
story: On November 14, 2003, astronomers scanning the edge of our solar system spotted a faint, icy world that broke the rules of planetary science: 90377 Sedna. Roughly 1,000 kilometers wide and glowing deep red with hydrocarbon sludge called tholins, Sedna travels on a dizzyingly elongated orbit. At its closest, it comes within 76 astronomical units of the Sun—far beyond Neptune—before plunging out to over 900 astronomical units, deep into the inner Oort cloud. It takes more than 10,000 years to complete just one loop. Because Neptune is too far away to have kicked Sedna into this bizarre trajectory, scientists realized something else had to be responsible. Sedna may be an ancient relic tugged by a sibling star in the Sun's newborn nursery, a world stolen from an alien star, or evidence of a massive, unseen Planet Nine shepherding the darkest fringes of our solar system.
angle: Sedna orbits so unimaginably far from the Sun that it takes over 11,000 years to complete a single trip, spending most of its journey in an extreme deep freeze far beyond the gravitational reach of any known planet.

claims.claim: Sedna was discovered on November 14, 2003, by astronomers Mike Brown, Chad Trujillo, and David Rabinowitz.
The discovery was made using the Samuel Oschin telescope at Palomar Observatory.
Before its formal naming, the object received the provisional designation 2003 VB12.
The dwarf planet was named after Sedna, the Inuit goddess of the sea.
When discovered, Sedna was approximately 90 AU from the Sun, making it the most distant observed body in the solar system at the time.
Sedna's closest orbital distance to the Sun (perihelion) is roughly 76 astronomical units.
Sedna's aphelion carries it to an extreme distance of over 900 astronomical units from the Sun.
Sedna takes over 10,000 years to complete a single orbit around the Sun.
Sedna never enters the Kuiper belt and never comes close enough to be gravitationally scattered by Neptune.
Sedna is regarded as an inner Oort cloud object and became the prototype of a class of objects called sednoids.
Sedna will reach its next closest approach to the Sun (perihelion) in the year 2076.
Sedna has a diameter estimated at approximately 1,000 kilometers.
Sedna's visible surface is exceptionally red, ranking among the reddest known objects in the Solar System.
Sedna's deep red coloration is attributed to complex organic hydrocarbon compounds known as tholins.
Early suspicions that Sedna had a moon slowing its spin were refuted when Hubble Space Telescope observations detected no satellites.
Sedna rotates on its axis once every approximately 10 hours.
One leading hypothesis proposes that Sedna was perturbed into its orbit by a close encounter with a passing star in the Sun's birth cluster.
Another hypothesis suggests that Sedna was captured or stolen by the Sun from a passing alien star system.
In 2012, astronomers discovered 2012 VP113, a second object on a similar detached high-perihelion orbit.
The shared orbital clustering of Sedna and other extreme trans-Neptunian objects led astronomers to hypothesize the existence of Planet Nine.

disputed: Orbital period: S1 and S7 give ~11,400 years, S2 calculates 10,663 years, S3 states 10,500 years, and S5 gives 12,050 years; a script should state 'over 10,000 years' or 'roughly 11,000 years'.

Diameter: Early estimates placed the size between 1,600 and 2,200 km, but Spitzer, Herschel, and occultation observations later narrowed it to roughly 900–1,000 km; scripts should clarify that earlier estimates were revised downward.
Rotation period: Early reports hypothesized a 20-to-50-day period caused by a moon, but subsequent telescope data proved it rotates in about 10 hours without any detected moon.

Surface ice detections: S5 states Sedna shows no clear signs of surface ices, while S1 documents detections of water, methane, and ethane ices; script should follow newer spectroscopic findings or attribute the detection history.

Origin scenario: Sources offer multiple competing hypotheses (stellar encounter in the Sun's birth cluster, capture from an alien star, or shepherding by an unseen massive Planet Nine); scripts should present these as competing theories rather than settled fact.
